title: Remotes: the shared copy
objective: By the end of this lesson you can clone a project, understand what origin actually is, and read the difference between your branches and the ones on the server.

blocks.text: Everything so far worked on your machine alone. A remote is another copy of the same repository that you have agreed to synchronise with — usually one hosted somewhere everyone can reach. Nothing about Git changes when you add one; you simply gain a way to exchange commits.

blocks.caption: Getting a copy
lines: # You now have: the full history, all branches, and a remote named 'origin'

blocks.title: origin is a nickname, not a rule
blocks.text: Git names the remote you cloned from 'origin' by convention. It has no special powers — it is a short name for a URL. A project can have several remotes, which is how you work with a fork and the original at the same time.
Three kinds of branch, which is where confusion starts

rows: Your last-known snapshot of the server's main
The actual state on the remote

blocks.text: origin/main is not live. It is a note your machine made the last time it talked to the server. When someone says 'my branch is behind', they mean their local branch has fewer commits than that note — and the note itself may already be out of date.

blocks.caption: Seeing all three
lines: git fetch origin      # update the notes without changing your work
git status            # now tells you ahead/behind accurately

blocks.title: fetch is always safe
blocks.text: It downloads commits and updates your remote-tracking notes, and touches nothing you are working on. When you are unsure of the situation, fetch first and then look — it is the read-only half of pull.

blocks.caption: Common operations
lines: git remote add origin https://github.com/org/project.git   # connect an existing local repo
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original/project.git  # the fork pattern
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:org/project.git   # switch to SSH

rows: Generate a key and add the public half to the host
Asks for a token unless a credential helper stores it

blocks.title: The password prompt is not a password anymore
blocks.text: Major hosts stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations years ago. If HTTPS asks you to authenticate, it wants a personal access token — treat that token like a credential, give it the narrowest scope that works, and never paste it into a file the repository tracks.

blocks.caption: When the default is too much
lines: git clone --depth 1 <url>          # only the latest commit — fast, no usable history
git clone --branch release <url>   # start on a specific branch
git clone <url> my-folder          # clone into a different directory name

blocks.text: A shallow clone is right for a build server that only needs current files. It is wrong for your own work, because most of what makes Git useful — log, blame, bisect — needs the history you just declined to download.

blocks.title: Work with a remote you control
steps: Create a bare repository to act as a server: git init --bare ~/git-server/demo.git
Clone it as if you were a colleague: git clone ~/git-server/demo.git ~/git-lab-clone
In the clone: git log --oneline   (the whole history came with it)
blocks.expected: A local repository connected to a remote you own, a push that succeeds, and a second clone containing the complete history — the same model as a hosted service, with no account required.

cheatsheet: A remote is another copy of the same repository you sync with
origin is just the conventional nickname for the URL you cloned from
main = yours · origin/main = your last-known note of the server · the server has its own
git fetch updates the notes and changes nothing you are working on — always safe
git branch -r lists remote-tracking branches; -a lists everything
git remote add <name> <url> connects a repository to a remote
SSH for anything you push regularly; HTTPS needs a token, not a password
--depth 1 is for build servers, not for work that needs log, blame, or bisect

choices.A: A live view of the server's main branch, always up to date
choices.B: Your local note of where the server's main branch was
choices.C: The branch you are currently on
choices.D: A backup of your local main

checkpoint.explanation: Fetch and pull update it, and a successful push may update the associated remote-tracking ref too. It remains a local note rather than a live server view, so it can be stale until the next communication.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is git fetch considered safe to run at any time?

choices.A: It updates remote-tracking branches, never your work
choices.B: It only reads the first commit
choices.D: It creates a full backup before running, so nothing can be lost

checkpoint.explanation: Fetch is the read-only half of pull. It changes what you know, not what you have. It also downloads the new commits — but never touches your working files or your branch.

checkpoint.prompt: HTTPS prompts you for a password when pushing. What does it actually want?

choices.B: Your account password, which is easier to rotate
choices.D: A personal access token with minimal scope

checkpoint.explanation: Major hosts stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations. A token is a credential — scope it tightly and never commit it. 'Minimal' means the narrowest scope that still works.

checkpoint.prompt: When is git clone --depth 1 the wrong choice?

choices.B: On a build server that only compiles the current code

checkpoint.explanation: Log, blame, and bisect all need the history it skips. A shallow clone trades away exactly the capabilities that make Git worth using day to day.
